newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: French, rebels exchange fire in Bangui-witnesses.
newsitem.headline: French, rebels exchange fire in Bangui-witnesses.

text.p: French troops based in the Central African Republic exchanged fire on Thursday with mutinous local soldiers who still control parts of the capital Bangui despite a four-day-old truce, witnesses said.
There were no immediate reports of casualties from the clash lasting about half an hour in Bangui's Kpetene district.

The witnesses said the French came under fire when they tried to go through a rebel barricade on a road leading to the country's main petrol depot in the district. French troops fired back from armoured vehicles.
Rebels handed over the depot to French control on Tuesday after holding it since the start of the mutiny on Novemver 16.
There was no imediate comment from the Bangui French command, the rebels or loyalist local forces.

French troops intervened last May to keep President Ange-Felix Patasse in power during a violent uprising by his army. Soldiers revolted earlier in April over pay grievances that carried over into the latest unrest.
The French, who are based in the former colony under bilateral accords, have maintained a low profile this time, restricting their role to protection of key locations.

Thursday's incident happened as Mali's former military ruler General Amadou Toumani Toure was due in Bangui to follow up regional mediation initiated last week by the presidents of Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon and Mali.

The mutineers hardened their original pay demands into a political campaign to unseat Patasse, who won elections in 1993. The mutiny turned into a bloody feud between Patasse's northern Baya tribe and southern Yakomas who dominate the army.
The four heads of state were mandated by the Franco-African summit in Burkina Faso last week to try and prevent civil war.
Most shops and businesses closed at the height of the violence have reopened since the start of the 15-day truce on Sunday but government offices remain shut.
Roadblocks diviting the capital into tribal no-go areas also remain in place.
